title_fr: Effectifs militaires terrestres des sept puissances jouables, 1914 (MIL-01)
status: BASE DE RECHERCHE. Chaque valeur porte sa source, sa page, sa définition et sa fiabilité. Aucune valeur n'est inventée : une donnée introuvable vaut null avec le motif. Les RÉPARTITIONS territoriales et la ventilation hors carte sont des ESTIMATIONS documentées (méthode dans docs/history/MIL01_METHODE.md), pas des faits historiques.

model._statut: Modèle VALIDÉ par le directeur (mission du 15/11/2026, §4.1) : (A) armée active ; (B) réserves mobilisables ; le jeu distingue en outre : en cours de mobilisation, incorporés, présents dans les unités.
model.active: Officiers et hommes sous les drapeaux au début de la campagne, en temps de paix (avant la mobilisation de fin juillet 1914).
model.reserves: Hommes instruits susceptibles d'être rappelés à la mobilisation, non présents dans les unités au départ.

normalisation.rule: Une seule définition par catégorie pour les sept puissances.
normalisation.active_definition: Effectif du temps de paix de l'armée de terre régulière « officiers et hommes sous les drapeaux » (US War Dept 1916, tableau p. 9 : « Only officers and men with colors are considered »), juillet 1914 ou budget 1914. Exclus : réserves, milices territoriales non présentes, troupes coloniales et indigènes servant hors d'Europe.
normalisation.reserves_definition: « Fully trained reserves available for passing from peace to war footing » (US War Dept 1916, tableau p. 9), estimation de 1911, PLAFONNÉE par le total des instruits de la rubrique « Total war strength » de la fiche nationale du même document, diminué de l'armée active (règle de cohérence de phase 1, 15/11/2026 : actif + réserves ne peut dépasser le total de la source). Le plafond s'applique à l'Allemagne et à l'Italie ; il est sans effet pour la France (3,8 M) et la Russie (6,0 M) ; il n'est pas appliqué à l'Autriche-Hongrie, dont le total (« fully trained men subject to call ») désigne des hommes à rappeler, donc hors actifs. Pour le Royaume-Uni, Army Reserve + Special Reserve au 1er août 1914 (War Office 1922) ; pour l'Empire ottoman, estimation de l'état-major ottoman rapportée par Erickson.
normalisation.why: Le document américain applique la même définition à six des sept armées, à une date unique (juillet 1914). Les sources nationales, plus précises pour un pays, emploient des définitions différentes (effectif budgétaire, Friedenspräsenzstärke sans officiers, armée métropolitaine avec ou sans Algérie, armée commune sans Landwehr...). Elles sont conservées comme DIVERGENCES et servent de contrôle.
normalisation.known_bias: Les chiffres de réserves du document américain datent de 1911 ; le document précise que les augmentations postérieures n'ont pas été rendues publiques (p. 9). Ce sont donc des minimums probables.

US_WD_1916.citation: United States War Department, Office of the Chief of Staff, War College Division, General Staff, No. 22 : Strength and Organization of the Armies of France, Germany, Austria, Russia, England, Italy, Mexico and Japan (Showing Conditions in July, 1914). Washington, Government Printing Office, 1916 (War Department Document No. 499).
US_WD_1916.type: publication officielle contemporaine (renseignement militaire d'un État neutre)
US_WD_1916.reliability_note: Source unique et homogène pour six armées, datée de juillet 1914. L'introduction avertit : « no accurate estimate can be given of the real fighting force of these nations as it existed at the outbreak of the war » (p. 5) et que les chiffres de mobilisation sont des minimums. Le tableau p. 9 a été contrôlé sur le fac-similé (PDF p. 15). Relu le 15/11/2026 (phase 1) : chaque fiche nationale comporte une rubrique « TOTAL WAR STRENGTH » (Allemagne p. 28, France p. 20, Autriche-Hongrie p. 37-38, Russie p. 45-46, Italie p. 66), distincte du tableau p. 9.

WO_1922.citation: War Office, Statistics of the Military Effort of the British Empire during the Great War, 1914-1920. Londres, HMSO, mars 1922.
WO_1922.reliability_note: Tableau (i)(b) p. 30 (PDF p. 40) et Section 10 p. 156-157 (PDF p. 168-169), contrôlés sur le fac-similé. Relu le 15/11/2026 (phase 1) sur l'image de la p. 30 (archive.org, page n39) : Territorial Force 10 684 officiers + 258 093 hommes = 268 777, avec la note † « Includes permanent staff of the Territorial Force ». Relu en phase 4 (15/11/2026) : p. 25-26 (commandements et divisions territoriales, avril 1920) dans le texte OCR ; p. 153 (Section 8) sur l'image du fac-similé.

ERICKSON_2000.citation: Edward J. Erickson, « Turkey Prepares for War, 1913-1914 », Relevance: The Quarterly Journal of the Great War Society, printemps 2000. Repris sur le blog Roads to the Great War, 7 janvier 2019.
ERICKSON_2000.type: article d'un historien spécialiste (auteur de Ordered to Die, 2001), consulté dans une reprise en ligne
ERICKSON_2000.reliability_note: Chiffres arrondis ; pagination de l'article original non disponible. À recouper avec Erickson, Ordered to Die (Greenwood, 2001), annexe sur l'organisation de 1914.

BUNDESARCHIV.citation: Bundesarchiv, « Preußische und deutsche Streitkräfte 1867 bis 1918 », guide thématique, rubrique Personalumfang.
BUNDESARCHIV.reliability_note: Chiffres arrondis, sans définition détaillée ni distinction claire entre armée prussienne et contingents bavarois, saxon et wurtembergeois.

BERNHARDI_1914.citation: Friedrich von Bernhardi, « Das Heerwesen », dans Deutschland unter Kaiser Wilhelm II., t. I, Berlin, Reimar Hobbing, 1914, p. 3-24 (Wikisource).
BERNHARDI_1914.type: texte contemporain d'un général (source primaire publiée)

WO_HANDBOOK_DE_1914.citation: General Staff, War Office, Handbook of the German Army (Home and Colonial), 4e éd. 1912, amendée en août 1914.

HQ_GENERAL_KNOWLEDGE.citation: Sièges des commandements de corps du temps de paix : connaissance encyclopédique courante (articles de corps d'armée de Wikipédia et ouvrages d'ordre de bataille), NON revérifiée siège par siège pendant la mission.
HQ_GENERAL_KNOWLEDGE.reliability_note: N'affecte que la répartition territoriale estimée. Les sièges confirmés par une source consultée portent hq_verification = « vérifié ».

RU_RASPISANIE_1914.citation: Главный штаб, Краткое расписание сухопутных войск. Исправлено по сведениям к 1-му марта 1914 г. Санкт-Петербург, 1914 (état abrégé officiel des troupes de terre de l'Empire russe, à jour au 1er mars 1914).
RU_RASPISANIE_1914.type: publication officielle de l'état-major russe (source primaire)
RU_RASPISANIE_1914.reliability_note: Section « Гвардейский, Гренадерский и армейские корпуса », p. 214-226 : une notice par corps, close par « Штабъ г. … » (siège de l'état-major). Lue dans le texte OCR d'archive.org (orthographe pré-1918, OCR imparfait) ; les 27 corps européens y figurent. Date : 1er mars 1914, deux mois après le départ de la campagne (T-057).

SEC_west_EB1911_BE.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 3, article 'Belgium', section 'Defence' / army. Standard contemporary reference summarising the 1909 conscription law, the active army, the reserve, the Garde Civique and the Brialmont fortified positions (Antwerp, Liège, Namur). Reliable for structure and order of magnitude; peacetime headcounts are only approximate.
SEC_west_EB1911_BE.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official returns

SEC_west_EB1911_NL.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 17, article 'Netherlands' (or 'Holland'), section 'Defence' / army. Describes conscription (introduced 1898-1901), short service with the colours, the reserve/Landsturm, the small peace establishment, the two field divisions and the defence system of the New Dutch Water Line and the Stelling van Amsterdam.
SEC_west_EB1911_NL.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official returns

SEC_west_EB1911_LU.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), article 'Luxemburg'/'Luxembourg', section 'Defence'. Notes the Grand Duchy's perpetual neutrality under the 1867 Treaty of London, the demolition of the fortress of Luxembourg and the existence of only a very small armed force. Reliable for the qualitative picture, not for exact numbers.
SEC_west_EB1911_LU.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official returns

SEC_west_EB1911_CH.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), article 'Switzerland', section 'Defence'. Describes the Swiss militia system: no standing army, recruit schools and refresher courses, the active levy / Landwehr / Landsturm, the small permanent instructional cadre and the large trained manpower pool. Reliable for structure; simultaneous under-arms headcounts are not given directly.
SEC_west_EB1911_CH.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official returns

SEC_west_SYB1914.citation: Statesman's Year-Book, 1914 edition (ed. J. Scott Keltie), national entries for Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg and Switzerland, sections 'Defence' / 'Army'. The annual compilation of official government returns closest in date to January 1914; the standard reference for peace establishments of the European armies. Used here for order-of-magnitude and structure; exact figures could not be re-verified in this environment (see METHODOLOGY).
SEC_west_SYB1914.type: contemporary annual statistical compilation of official returns

SEC_west_USWD1916.citation: U.S. War Department, War College Division, 'Strength and Organization of the Armies of the European Powers' (Washington, Government Printing Office, 1916) and related War Department handbooks of 1916-1918. Official contemporary compilation contrasting peace (under-arms) strength, trained reserve and war establishment of European armies. Used only as a cross-check for orders of magnitude, not for exact figures; dated after January 1914.

SEC_west_METHODOLOGY.citation: Research note. No web-search or web-fetch access was available for this task (the search tool is failing in this environment). All figures were reconstructed from established historical knowledge of the standard references cited above (EB1911 national articles, Statesman's Year-Book 1913/1914, US War Department 1916 handbooks and national military handbooks). Where the sources do not permit a precise, dated headcount the numbers are explicitly labelled as ESTIMATES, with a stated range in the divergences. The four categories are kept strictly separate: (1) theoretical/establishment strength, (2) troops actually under arms in peace time (the 'active' value), (3) trained reservists available (the 'reserves' value), (4) wartime mobilised strength (recorded only in divergences/notes, never as peace-time active strength).

SEC_balkans_US_WD_1916.citation: United States, War Department, General Staff, 'Handbook of the Balkan States: Servia, Montenegro, Albania, Bulgaria, Greece, and European Turkey', Government Printing Office, Washington, 1916 (prepared by George F. Andrews). Contemporary official compilation based largely on pre-1914/1914 data.
SEC_balkans_US_WD_1916.note: REFERENCE ONLY: full text could NOT be retrieved. Retries on 2026-11-17: Internet Archive /stream/..._djvu.txt returned 404; archive.org advancedsearch found no item titled 'Handbook of the Balkan States' ( nor any 1916 US War Department item); Google Books API returned HTTP 429 (rate-limited); websearch unavailable. No page-specific figure below is attributed to it directly; it is listed because it is the standard contemporary source the lead requested. If a future agent can access it, it is the single most valuable source for contemporary (c.1913-14) gendarmerie/army returns, especially for Albania and Montenegro.

SEC_balkans_EB1911_SERVIA.citation: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, vol. 24, article 'Servia' (partly by Chedomille Mijatovich), section 'Defence': national army of 5 divisions (HQ Nish, Belgrade, Valyevo, Kraguyevats, Zayechar); 'On a peace footing the strength of the army is 35,000 men; in war it might reach 225,000, including landsturm.' Text VERIFIED VERBATIM from the Wikisource transcription (page ID 3409122) on 2026-11-17: 'The defensive force of the country, as reorganized in 1901, consists of the national army (narodna voyska) and the landsturm... On a peace footing the strength of the army is 35,000 men; in war it might reach 225,000, including landsturm.' It also states the modern forts of Nish, Pirot and Zayechar were strengthened/re-armed in the early 20th century.

SEC_balkans_EB1911_BULGARIA.citation: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, vol. 4, article 'Bulgaria' by James David Bourchier, subsection 'Army and Navy': organisation based on law of 1 Jan 1904; peace strength 1905 = 2,500 officers + 48,200 men; 9 infantry divisions with divisional HQs at Sofia, Philippopolis, Sliven, Shumla, Rustchuk, Vratza, Plevna, Stara-Zagora, Dupnitza; war strength active army + reserve 180,954; reserve army + opltchenie brings grand total to about 338,000 officers and men.

SEC_balkans_EB1911_GREECE.citation: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, vol. 12, article 'Greece' (Bourchier et al.), section 'Army': 1904 reorganisation scheme peace footing 1,887 officers + 25,140 NCOs and men, war active army >=120,000 plus territorial army >=60,000; 'In 1908 ... peace strength ... 1939 officers and civilians, 19,416 non-commissioned officers and men ... reserves will furnish about 77,000 men and the territorial army about 37,000 men in time of war.'

SEC_balkans_EB1911_MONTENEGRO.citation: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, vol. 18, article 'Montenegro' by James David Bourchier, section 'Defence': 'There is a standing corps of officers, but no standing army'; 11 infantry brigades, 56 battalions; 'The war strength is estimated at from 38,000 to 42,000 men' (first ban ~32,000, second ban/reserve 5,000-6,000, artillery ~1,500); 20,000-22,000 men of military age absent abroad; 'About 20,000 men can concentrate at a given spot within 48 hours'; permanent corps of 20 perianiki (1907); arsenal at Spuzh.

SEC_balkans_HALL_BALKAN.citation: Richard C. Hall, 'The Balkan Wars, 1912-1913: Prelude to the First World War' (Routledge, 2000), pp. 16, 18, as quoted in Wikipedia 'Bulgarian Land Forces' (quote VERIFIED 2026-11-17 in article section 'Early years'): Bulgarian peacetime force of 60,000 expanded to 370,000 in war (more than half the League's 700,000), 'with almost 600,000 men mobilised in total, out of a population of 4,300,000'; field army of 9 infantry divisions, 1 cavalry division and 1,116 artillery pieces.

SEC_balkans_WIKI_BALKAN_WARS.citation: Wikipedia, 'Balkan Wars', infobox strengths: First Balkan War - Bulgaria 600,000+, Serbia 230,000, Greece 125,000, Montenegro 44,500; Second Balkan War - Bulgaria 450,000+, Serbia 348,000, Greece 148,000, Montenegro 12,800. These are WARTIME (1912-13) figures, not peace establishment.

SEC_balkans_WIKI_HELLENIC_ARMY.citation: Wikipedia, 'Hellenic Army', section 'Decade of wars: 1912-1922': French military mission 1911-1914; 'while foreign observers estimated a mobilized force of approximately 50,000 men, the Army eventually fielded 125,000, with another 140,000 in the National Guard and reserves.'

SEC_balkans_WIKI_ROYAL_SERBIAN_ARMY.citation: Wikipedia, 'Royal Serbian Army': infobox size 420,000, citing vojska.net ('Serbian army, August 1914') and Thomas & Babac, 'Armies in the Balkans 1914-1918', p. 12. This is a wartime mobilisation figure.

SEC_balkans_VOJSKA_SERBIA_1914.citation: Vojska.net (Ivan Bajlo), 'Serbian army, August 1914': Commander-in-Chief Prince Aleksandar, Chief of Staff vojvoda Putnik; 420,597 soldiers (about 250,000 frontline, about 150,000 rear echelon), 71,200 horses; 1st, 2nd, 3rd Armies plus Timok, Užice and detachment groupings; infantry divisions Timok I/II, Morava I/II, Šumadija I, Danube I, Drina I/II, Combined Division I, Cavalry Division.

SEC_balkans_VOJSKA_MNE_1914.citation: Vojska.net (Ivan Bajlo), 'Montenegro army, August 1914': Commander-in-Chief King Nikola, Chief of Staff General Božidar Janković, HQ Cetinje; Pljevlja division ~6,000 (10 bns), Herzegovina detachment ~15,000 (15 bns), Lovćen detachment ~8,000 (18 bns), Starosrbijanski detachment ~6,000 (13 bns) - total ~35,000 in 56 battalions.

SEC_balkans_WIKI_ALBANIAN_AF.citation: Wikipedia, 'Albanian Armed Forces': Albanian National Army formed 4 December 1912 by Ismail Qemali's provisional government, first commander Lt. Col. Ali Shefqet Shkupi; next numerical strength quoted is 10,691 active troops in 1923, i.e. no reliable contemporary 1914 return is given.

SEC_balkans_WIKI_BULGARIAN_LAND.citation: Wikipedia, 'Bulgarian Land Forces', section 'Early years': citing Hall (2000) - Bulgarian army 'militarily the most powerful of the four states'; peacetime force 60,000 expanded to 370,000 in the First Balkan War, almost 600,000 mobilised in total from a population of 4,300,000; field army 9 infantry divisions, 1 cavalry division.

SEC_iberia_SYB1913.citation: The Statesman's Year-Book: Statistical and Historical Annual of the States of the World for the Year 1913. Spain: 'Defence — Army', pp. 1260-1262; Portugal: 'Defence', pp. 1151-1152. Figures 'revised after official returns'.
SEC_iberia_SYB1913.type: contemporary statistical year-book based on official government returns (primary/near-primary published source)

SEC_iberia_WWI1916.citation: Ángel Alcalde, 'Military and Strategy (Spain)', in 1914-1918-online. International Encyclopedia of the First World War, ed. Ute Daniel et al., Freie Universität Berlin, 9 June 2017, DOI 10.15463/ie1418.11108 (peer-reviewed academic article). Cites Romanones, Reformas Militares (1915), pp.25-33 and La Porte, 'La espiral irresistible', Hispania Nova 15 (2017), pp.500-526.
SEC_iberia_WWI1916.type: peer-reviewed academic encyclopedia article with cited primary and secondary sources

SEC_iberia_NYT1914.citation: The New York Times, 29 October 1914, 'PORTUGAL'S ARMY 130,000.; With 50,000 in the Territorial Reserve' — 'When mobilization is ordered, after allowing for wastage, the number of fully trained men in the active army and its two reserves amounts to about 130,000, with perhaps 50,000 men of the territorial reserve...' (headline and lead retrieved via search index; full text paywalled).
SEC_iberia_NYT1914.type: contemporary newspaper report of official/ War Office estimates, October 1914 (wartime context)

SEC_iberia_HCPT.citation: 'Portuguese Armed Forces. Details of Strength, Dispositions and Quality' (British military intelligence summary, reproduced by History Commons): troops 'with colours including National Republican Guard and Police is estimated at 44,000, (to which must be added about 10,000 men in the colonies)'; 'In peace there is no divisional organisation. In war it is intended to mobilise five infantry divisions on outbreak, with an ultimate mobilisation of a further twelve divisions.' (Text available only as a search-index excerpt; site behind Cloudflare.)
SEC_iberia_HCPT.type: British War Office-style intelligence handbook / summary (contemporary, exact date not verified)

SEC_iberia_WORLDARMY.citation: 'World Armies' (compiled reference), section 'F. The Spanish Army in 1914', listing I-VIII Corps Districts and overseas commands (Melilla, Ceuta, Canaries, Balearics) and the 1914 regiment/corps inventory. PDF p.93 (printed p.318).
SEC_iberia_WORLDARMY.type: secondary compiled reference work (order of battle detail; no troop-strength figures in the accessible section)

SEC_iberia_WIKI.citation: Wikipedia, 'Spanish Army' / 'Portuguese Army' / 'Spain during World War I' / 'Portugal during World War I' — used only for territorial district names, 1911 Portuguese reorganisation and general contextual facts, not for strength figures.
SEC_iberia_WIKI.type: tertiary encyclopedia, used for cross-checking organisation only

SEC_nordic_EB1911_RO.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 23, article 'Rumania' (Arthur J. Evans, Henry Trotter, Moses Gaster), section 'Defence'. Gives the 1891 conscription law (modified 1900, 1908), three military sections (field army and reserves ages 21-30; territorial militia ages 30-36; Gloata/Landsturm ages 36-46), four army corps at Craiova, Bucharest, Jassy, Galatz, an independent Dobrudja brigade and a cavalry division at Bucharest; peace strength 1909-10 = 4,415 officers + 89,227 NCOs and men + 18,920 horses; war footing of field army 225,000 combatants; projected militia 100,000 (not fully organised by 1910).
SEC_nordic_EB1911_RO.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official statistics

SEC_nordic_EB1911_DK.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 8, article 'Denmark', section 'Army and Navy'. Gives active army composition (Life Guard battalion, 10 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 5 cavalry regiments of 3 squadrons, 12 field batteries, 3 fortress artillery battalions, 6 engineer companies); peace strength of permanent troops 13,500 officers and men; annual contingent trained 2-3 years with colours 22,500; annual special-reservist contingent 17,000; up to 75,000 under arms at peak periods, average nearly 60,000; c.80,000 reservists given refresher training in 1907; war footing field army c.50,000, more than doubled by reserves, nearly 120,000 with the colours in 1907 manoeuvres.
SEC_nordic_EB1911_DK.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official statistics

SEC_nordic_EB1911_NO.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 19, article 'Norway' (Philip Lake, Osbert J. R. Howarth, Bertha S. Phillpotts, Hans L. Brækstad, Edmund Gosse), section 'Army and Navy'. Army = line + landværn (reserve) + landstorm (second reserve); conscription from 22, 6 years line, 6 reserve, 4 second reserve; war liability ages 18-50; peace establishment of the line 12,000 men with 750 officers; war footing 26,000 or more but not above 18,000 without parliamentary authority; only fortress garrisons and the Christiania garrison of Norwegian Guards are enlisted troops; principal fortresses Oscarsborg, Agdenes, Bergen, Tönsberg, Christiansand.
SEC_nordic_EB1911_NO.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official statistics

SEC_nordic_EB1911_SE.citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), vol. 26, article 'Sweden' (Frederick Beck, Robert Nisbet Bain, Oskar Dumrath, Osbert Howarth, Edmund Gosse), section 'Army and Navy'. Universal military service; conscripts aged 21-40, 8 years first levy, 4 second levy, 8 reserves; 1901 law set 240 days infantry etc., 365 days cavalry/field artillery; permanent cadres c.22,000; c.85,000 men trained annually as recruits or recalled; peace organisation 82 infantry battalions (28 regiments), 50 cavalry squadrons, 71 field and 7 position artillery batteries, 10 fortress artillery, 16 engineer, 18 army service corps companies; 6 divisions quartered at Helsingborg, Linköping, Sköfde, Stockholm (two), Hernösand plus Gotland troops at Visby; c.500,000 men estimated available for service in case of war; fortresses Stockholm (Vaxholm, Oscar-Fredriksborg), Boden, Karlsborg, Karlskrona.
SEC_nordic_EB1911_SE.type: contemporary general encyclopedia based on official statistics

SEC_nordic_TANK_DK.citation: Leander Jobse, 'Kingdom of Denmark (WW1)', Tank Encyclopedia, 10 May 2011 [10 May 2021], section 'War time': Danish Army mobilised 1 August 1914; 'the peace-time force of 13,500 men had grown to a force of 47,000 men' six days later, 'further increasing to 58,000 men by the end of 1914'; only 10,000 on the Jutland border, remainder at Copenhagen; reduced to 34,000 conscripts by end 1915 and 24,500 in second half 1917. Article cites Danish archives and academic works (Christensen 2012; Sørensen 2014; Baltzersen 2005).

SEC_nordic_GLOBALSEC_DK.citation: GlobalSecurity.org, 'Denmark - Army - History': 'The peace strength of the Danish army was only about 14,000 men and officers, but a national militia system in which exemptions were very rare, somewhat after the Swiss style, was in vogue.'

SEC_nordic_WIKI_RO_CAMPAIGN.citation: Wikipedia, 'Romania in World War I' (consulted 2026): infobox gives Romanian mobilised strength in 1916 as 658,088 (plus 30,000 Russians, 20,000 Serbs, 1,600 French); text notes c.700,000 in June 1917 in 207 infantry battalions, 110 cavalry squadrons, 245 artillery batteries. Wartime figures, not January 1914.

SEC_nordic_WIKI_RO_ARMY.citation: Wikipedia, 'Romanian Land Forces': Second Balkan War 1913 - c.330,000 troops mobilised; Romanian army entered war 27 August 1916. Useful only for wartime comparison.

SEC_nordic_SPARTACUS_RO.citation: Spartacus Educational, 'The Romanian Army and the First World War' (John Simkin): 'Romania's peacetime army was manned by limited conscription, and all adult males spent time in the territorial reserve. This gave it a regular strength of around 100,000 men. On the outbreak of the Second Balkan War in 1913, conscription was introduced and the army grew to 400,000.'

SEC_nordic_WIKI_NO_ARMY.citation: Wikipedia, 'Norwegian Army', sections 'Independence' and 'World War I' (text derived from an early-20th-century encyclopedic description of the post-1920 militia system): six brigades established 1911, called divisions from 1916; 56 infantry battalions, 5 cyclist (ski) companies, 3 cavalry regiments (16 squadrons), 27 four-gun field batteries, 3 mountain batteries, 9 heavy artillery batteries, 1 engineer regiment and 2 battalions; 'The total peace strength was 118,500 men and comprised 71,836 rifles, 228 field and 36 heavy guns. The additional numbers available on mobilization amount to 282,000 men.' Liability 18-56, 12 years line then 12 years landvern then landstorm; initial training 48-102 days by arm. Note: this description is of the c.1920 'national militia' system and must not be read as troops continuously under arms.

SEC_nordic_WIKI_SE_ARMY.citation: Wikipedia, 'Swedish Army', section 'Size': 'Between the introduction of universal conscription in 1902 until the start of World War II, the army was usually maintained at a consistent strength of 100,000 men, with two-thirds of the force being conscripts for two years'; also notes army on active service consisted mainly of conscripts in basic training and refreshers.

SEC_nordic_WIKI_SE_WW1.citation: Wikipedia, 'Sweden during World War I' (good article), section 'Swedish military preparedness during the war - Army': 'During the entirety of the war, the active strength of the Swedish army never exceeded 13,000 men, even after the doubling in strength requested in Hammarskjöld's Army Bill of 1914 of reserve formations from six to twelve infantry divisions and a cavalry division'; by 1918 active deployable men fell as low as 2,000. Cites Qvarnström and Åselius (academic works).

SEC_nordic_NYT_SE.citation: New York Times, 2 August 1914, 'A NEW SWEDISH ARMY; Formidable Armament to be Based on Militia System': 'The regular peace footing will amount to 350,000 officers and men, with a pure militia reserve of about 500,000. Thus nearly 900,000 men can be put under arms at twelve hours' notice.' Contemporary press estimate, grossly inflated compared with official statistics; recorded only as a divergence.

SEC_nordic_CHORUS_NOTE.citation: Research note: the suggested US War Department 1916 army handbook could not be located as a freely accessible, verifiable online text during this research (archive.org and Google Books searches returned no usable item). Contemporary official-statistics-based figures were therefore taken principally from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica national articles, corroborated where possible by specialist/secondary sources. On 2026-11-17 all core figures for the four nations were re-verified against the complete EB1911 article texts on Wikisource (Rumania 'Defence'; Denmark 'Army and Navy'; Norway 'Army and Navy'; Sweden 'Army and Navy') and found consistent. All estimates are labelled as such.

secondary_research.organisation: Compulsory service under the law of 1909. Every Belgian was liable from about 19 to 40; the term with the colours was short (roughly 12-15 months by arm), followed by several years in the reserve and a territorial/Garde Civique obligation. In peacetime the army was small, organised in a handful of divisions; on mobilisation (August 1914) it expanded to six infantry divisions of roughly 12,000-15,000 men each, one cavalry division, and substantial fortress troops. The Garde Civique (civil guard) was a separate citizen militia used mainly for local defence and fortified-place duty. Fortifications designed by General Henri Brialmont guarded the Meuse at Liège and Namur and the great fortified camp of Antwerp, which served as the national redoubt. Infantry weapon: Mauser M1889, 7.65 mm; field artillery of 75 mm quick-firing type.
secondary_research.garrisons: Antwerp was the principal fortified camp and war-time refuge of the government and army (the 'national redoubt'), with large permanent and mobilised garrisons; Liège and Namur guarded the Meuse crossings with Brialmont forts; Brussels was the capital and location of the general staff and cavalry headquarters. Ghent, Bruges, Mons and Charleroi held recruiting and training depots in Flanders and the industrial Hainaut region. These HQs and the division-to-district mapping are approximate reconstructions; the peacetime provincial recruiting districts (one per province) do not map exactly onto the six mobilisation divisions.
uncertainties: No verified January 1914 daily return; the 33,000 active figure and 100,000 reserve figure are explicit estimates from the standard literature.
Whether Belgium maintained four or six divisions in being in peacetime is not firmly resolved here; the six divisions listed are the well-attested August 1914 field army.
The Garde Civique (c.40,000-50,000 nominal) is variously counted as part of the army or as a separate militia; it is excluded from both the active and the trained-reserve values.
Division and fortress-command headquarters are plausible rather than source-verified locations.
All August 1914 mobilisation figures are excluded from the peace-time values by design.

secondary_research.organisation: Conscription introduced in 1898-1901, with short service with the colours (infantry roughly 8-12 months, mounted and technical arms longer), followed by several years in the reserve and then the Landsturm. In peacetime the army was kept small: two field divisions, a cavalry brigade and fortress/garrison troops. On mobilisation it was to expand to roughly 200,000 men. The national defence plan rested on the New Dutch Water Line and the Stelling van Amsterdam (the fortified ring around the capital), with secondary fortified places at 's-Hertogenbosch, Nijmegen, Leeuwarden and Maastricht. The Dutch infantry of 1914 was armed with the Mannlicher M1895 magazine rifle (6.5 mm); the field artillery was being re-equipped with quick-firing guns. The Netherlands remained neutral and mobilised throughout the First World War.
secondary_research.garrisons: The main peacetime concentrations were around Amsterdam and The Hague/Rotterdam in Holland, which also held the headquarters of the two field divisions and the cavalry brigade. The Stelling van Amsterdam and the New Dutch Water Line were the keystones of defence, with Utrecht as the central water-line command. Regional garrisons and fortified places lay at 's-Hertogenbosch (North Brabant), Nijmegen (Gelderland), Leeuwarden (Friesland), Groningen and Maastricht (Limburg). These district locations are plausible reconstructions; the exact 1914 territorial command boundaries and headquarters are not verified here.
uncertainties: The 25,000 active and 175,000 reserve values are estimates; no exact January 1914 return was available for verification.
The total mobilised strength usually given for 1914 (c.200,000, sometimes c.250,000) is a wartime figure and is only used to derive the reserve estimate.
It is uncertain how much of the mobilised force was genuinely trained versus Landsturm, so 'trained reservists' is approximate.
Field-division and fortress-command headquarters are plausible rather than source-verified; the two-division peacetime field army is the best-attested structure.
The colonial army (KNIL) is excluded from the European land-force figures by design.

active.reference_date: January 1914 (peacetime militia training cycle; no standing army and no mobilisation until August 1914)
active.definition: Switzerland had NO standing army. The only troops actually under arms in peacetime were the small permanent instructional cadre (roughly 2,500-3,000 officers, NCOs and specialists) plus conscripts undergoing recruit school (Rekrutenschule) and men attending refresher courses (Wiederholungskurse). Averaged over the training year, on the order of 10,000-15,000 men were under arms at any one time; 12,000 is adopted here as a mid ESTIMATE. This is strictly distinct from the theoretical militia establishment (c.200,000 trained men, see reserves) and from the August 1914 mobilised army (c.200,000-250,000).

active.derivation: ESTIMATE. The cited references establish that there was no standing army and describe the recruit school and refresher-course system, but give no simultaneous daily headcount. secondary_research.organisation: Universal male conscription under the federal military organisation in force in 1914 (based on the 1907 army law and the federal constitution). Every Swiss male was liable from about 20 to 48: recruit school (roughly 90 days for infantry, longer for other arms) at about 20, followed by service in the active levy (Auszug), then the Landwehr and finally the Landsturm, with periodic refresher courses (Wiederholungskurse) in subsequent years. There was no standing army: the permanent cadre served as instructors, and units existed as trained formations whose men lived as civilians in peace. The field army was organised in six divisions plus cavalry and fortress troops. On mobilisation in August 1914 Switzerland fielded roughly 200,000-250,000 men to guard its frontiers, and total wartime strength approached 400,000 by 1918. Infantry weapon: Schmidt-Rubin magazine rifle, 7.5 mm.
secondary_research.garrisons: In peacetime the only permanently active elements were the general staff at Bern (the federal capital), the military schools and the cadres at the cantonal recruit-training centres; troops were not embodied in permanent garrisons. The six divisions were associated with cantonal recruiting areas covering the western (Geneva/Lausanne), northern (Basel/Zurich) and eastern (St Gallen/Graubünden/Tessin) frontiers. Fortress troops guarded the great alpine transit routes — Saint-Maurice, the Gotthard and the Grisons passes — and frontier brigades covered the Jura and the Rhine. Division and fortress headquarters are approximate reconstructions from cantonal military geography rather than verified 1914 returns.
uncertainties: The Swiss militia system makes 'active strength' definition-dependent: c.2,500-3,000 permanent cadre, c.10,000-15,000 under arms on an average day, and c.80,000-100,000 annual training throughput are all defensible readings; the 12,000 value is the simultaneous under-arms estimate.
The 190,000 reserve and c.200,000-250,000 mobilisation figures are estimates from the standard literature, not verified returns.
Whether Switzerland had six divisions in 1914, and the exact divisional recruiting areas and headquarters, are only approximately reconstructed here.
The c.400,000 wartime peak of 1918 is a later mobilisation figure and is excluded from all peace-time values.

secondary_research.organisation: Compulsory service under the law of 29 June 1911: total 18 years — 3 in the active army (generally reduced to 2), 3 in the first reserve, 6 in the second reserve, the remainder in an (as yet unorganised) territorial reserve. Metropolitan Spain was divided into 8 territorial districts, each under a Captain-General; districts I-VI each furnished 2 field divisions, districts VII-VIII one each (14 infantry divisions in all). A division comprised 2 infantry brigades of 2 regiments of 3 battalions (third battalion a cadre only in peace), 1 cavalry regiment, 1 field artillery regiment of 5 batteries, and 1 engineer regiment; batteries had 4 guns. Additional troops: 3 independent chasseur (cazador) brigades of 6 battalions, 4 mountain artillery regiments (14 batteries), 1 horse artillery regiment (5 batteries), 1 permanent cavalry division (2 brigades) and 3 permanent cavalry brigades. Wartime field army about 220,000 combatants. Second line: 116 infantry, 14 cavalry and 14 artillery cadres for 7 reserve divisions (~90,000). Guardia Civil (<20,000) and Carabineros (~15,000) were military-disciplined constabulary/customs corps. Infantry weapon: Mauser Model 1893, 7 mm (calibre .275); field gun: Schneider Canet 14.5-pdr.
secondary_research.garrisons: Distribution table (battalions/regiments, source SYB1913 p.1261): Spain 58 line infantry regiments, 15 chasseur battalions, 28 cavalry regiments, 18 field artillery, 7 horse/mountain, 6 garrison/siege; Africa (Melilla/Ceuta) 4, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1; Balearic Islands 4, 2, -, 1, -, 1; Canary Islands 4, 3, -, 1, -, 1. Totals 70 infantry regiments, 23 chasseur battalions, 29 cavalry, 19 field artillery, 13 other artillery, 7 fortress. The Army of Africa (Melilla, Ceuta, Larache, Alcazar) was nominally always on a war footing: corps of occupation of 12,000-15,000 combatants (4 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 3 cazador battalions of 6 companies, 1 cavalry regiment of 6 squadrons, 3 field batteries, 3-4 mountain batteries, 1 howitzer battery, 1 engineer regiment, native infantry/cavalry and police units). During 1913-14 the Rif War absorbed most Spanish field troops; WWI1916 states 75,000 troops (~60% of the army) were in Morocco at the outbreak of war in August 1914. Fortresses guarded the Pyrenees and Portuguese frontier (Pasajes, Santoña, Santander, Ferrol, A Coruña, Vigo, Tarifa, Algeciras, Cádiz).
uncertainties: The 128,073 figure is a peace ESTABLISHMENT including two paramilitary corps; the number of effectives actually present under arms in January 1914 is not separately given and was certainly somewhat lower.

The 1913 edition of the SYB is the closest accessible contemporary publication; the 1914 edition could not be located online. The conscription/establishment law did not change before July 1914, so the figures are treated as valid for January 1914, but this is an inference.

The 90,000 reserve figure is what could be organised into 7 second-line divisions; the total pool of men with reserve liability under the 1911 law was larger but unquantified and, for the territorial reserve, unorganised.
The 220,000 field army and the 75,000-in-Morocco figures are mobilisation/war-crisis numbers (July-August 1914 onward) and must not be used as January 1914 peace strengths.
WORLDARMY is a secondary compilation; SYB1913 and WWI1916 are preferred for numbers.

secondary_research.organisation: The Army of Portugal was a conscript militia. All males were liable from 17 to 45 (practically from 20): 10 years in the active army, 10 in the reserve, 5 in the territorial army (which also absorbed surplus men). Recruits underwent 15-30 weeks' preliminary training depending on arm, plus a fortnight's annual training. The country was divided into 3 territorial military districts (North, Centre, South), each expected to produce a division; each comprised two territorial divisions, and there were also the Azores and Madeira military commands plus the separate Lisbon Entrenched Camp command. The 1911 republican reform (January-May 1911) turned a largely professional army into a mainly militia army: the active troops comprised 8 divisions (each 4 infantry regiments, 1 machine-gun battery group, 1 mounted artillery regiment, 1 cavalry regiment) and a cavalry brigade of 3 regiments, plus non-divisional engineers, mountain/horse/howitzer artillery, 3 independent infantry regiments, machine-gun companies and services. In SYB terms: 35 infantry regiments of 3 battalions, 11 cavalry regiments of 4 squadrons, 8 field artillery regiments (63 batteries), 2 horse batteries, 9 mountain batteries, 20 garrison batteries and engineer units; batteries had 4 guns. Reserve army (cadres only in peace): 35 infantry regiments, 8 cavalry squadrons, 24 field batteries; territorial army had no cadres. Republican Guard ~5,000 (800 mounted) and Fiscal Guard ~5,200 were military-recruited civil corps usable in the field in war. Infantry arm: Mauser-Vergueiro 6.5 mm magazine rifle; field artillery rearming with 7.5 cm Schneider Canet guns. No general mobilisation before 1916.
secondary_research.garrisons: Metropolitan garrisons were spread among the three military districts and the Lisbon Entrenched Camp; the campaign/field organisation existed only on mobilisation (HCPT: 'In peace there is no divisional organisation'). Overseas: 2 line infantry regiments (2 battalions each) permanently stationed in the Azores and 1 at Madeira, with garrison artillery (1 battalion Madeira, 2 in the Azores). A separate Colonial Army garrisoned West Africa, Mozambique, India etc.: about 650 officers (partly seconded from the home army), about 2,500 European NCOs and men (volunteers) and about 7,000 native troops (compulsory) — roughly 10,150 total, consistent with HCPT's 'about 10,000 men in the colonies'. In August-October 1914 reinforcements (c.1,600 men to Angola, c.1,527 to Mozambique) were sent, but these are post-January-1914 movements.
uncertainties: The SYB1913 '30,000 men' active establishment may or may not include the ~2,800 officers; the 1914 unit structure from the 1911 reform is well attested but the exact peace-time headcount actually present is not.
The reserve figure (100,000) is a derived estimate from an October 1914 newspaper report of official estimates; the SYB gives only reserve order of battle, no strength. Treat as approximate.
The NYT headline figure of 130,000 applies to active plus two reserves combined after wastage — it is a mobilisation estimate, not a peace-time active strength.
The exact headquarters of the Centre Military District (Coimbra versus Lisbon) is not firmly established from the sources consulted.

HCPT (British intelligence summary) was accessible only as a search-index excerpt and its exact date is unverified; its broader 44,000 'with colours' figure should not be substituted for the SYB active establishment without qualification.
The 1913 edition of the SYB is the closest accessible contemporary publication; its military sections were still current in January 1914, but this is an inference rather than a 1914-dated return.

secondary_research.organisation: Militia/territorial-style conscription rather than a large standing army. Six brigades established in 1911 as district organisations, redesignated divisions by Army Order 1916; in 1914 they were still brigades. Each district was roughly a brigade (about four infantry battalions plus an artillery regiment) rather than a full division. Army order of c.1920: 56 infantry battalions, 5 cyclist/ski companies, 3 cavalry regiments (16 squadrons), 27 field batteries, 3 mountain batteries, 9 heavy artillery batteries, 1 engineer regiment and 2 battalions; a small flying corps. secondary_research.garrisons: Principal fortresses: Oscarsborg on Christiania Fjord, Agdenes at Trondhjem Fjord, Bergen, Tönsberg and Christiansand; Norwegian Guards garrison at Christiania. Main district centres at Christiania, Bergen, Trondhjem, Stavanger/Christiansand and northern Norway.

secondary_research.organisation: General conscription introduced in 1901-1902, replacing the old indelta (indelningsverket) system of military tenure every man between 21 and 40 served 8 years in the first levy, 4 in the second and 8 in the reserves. A war division would probably comprise 4 infantry regiments (12 battalions), 4 cavalry squadrons, 1 artillery regiment, 1 engineer company etc.; a cavalry division 2 brigades of 8 squadrons plus horse artillery. secondary_research.organisation: Conscription under the law of 1891 as modified in 1900 and 1908. Three sections: first section, men 21-30 in the field army and its reserves; second section, men 30-36 in the territorial militia; third section, men 36-46 in the Gloata (Landsturm) for home service only. Main army depots and the Danube/Black Sea naval bases at Galatz and Constantza.

secondary_research.organisation: Organisation under the law of 1 January 1904 (EB1911): (1) active or field army (deystvuyushta armia), subdivided into the active army and the active army reserve; (2) reserve army (reservna armia); (3) opltchenïe (militia, employed only inside the kingdom). Each divisional area was divided into 4 recruitment districts (36 total), each providing one 4-battalion regiment. Conscription: 2 years infantry + 8 years active reserve, or 3 years other arms + 6 years active reserve, then further militia liability. In the Balkan Wars the field army was 9 infantry divisions + 1 cavalry division.

secondary_research.organisation: Tribal militia system: 11 infantry brigades of 4-6 battalions each (56 battalions total), companies (tchete) raised by clan with their own standard-bearers. No cavalry. Artillery (1910): 18 siege, 25 field, 38 mountain guns, 4 howitzers, 15 mortars, 18 machine guns, mostly Russian-supplied; heavy guns at Spuž arsenal. In August 1914 the force was grouped as the Pljevlja Division, Herzegovina, Lovćen and Starosrbijanski (Old Serbia) detachments under King Nikola with General Božidar Janković as Chief of Staff (VOJSKA_MNE_1914).
secondary_research.garrisons: Cetinje (capital, royal residence, perianiki guard), Nikšić (artillery school and brigade, cathedral town), Podgorica (officer training school), Spuž (principal arsenal and heavy guns), Bar/Antivari and Dulcigno (coast), Pljevlja and Andrijevica (northern/ethnic frontier garrisons newly relevant after 1913 territorial gains).
uncertainties: DATA RELIABILITY EXPLICITLY LOW - no reliable contemporary order of battle or strength return for January 1914 was located.
EB1911 source is from c.1911, before the Balkan Wars; Montenegro's territory and population changed in 1912-13.
Contemporary figures (38,000-44,500 war strength) are theoretically possible mobilisation, not troops under arms in peace.
Mass emigration of military-age men (20,000-22,000) makes all manpower estimates highly speculative.
Vojska.net is a hobbyist site; its August 1914 figures should be treated as indicative only.
The Second Balkan War strength of 12,800 given by Wikipedia is contradicted by all other sources and is likely erroneous.

active.definition: Nominal gendarmerie and regular armed formations nominally under the provisional Albanian government - NOT a national army in the effective sense
active.derivation: Albania declared independence 28 November 1912; the Albanian National Army was created 4 December 1912 under Ismail Qemali (first commander Lt. Col. Ali Shefqet Shkupi). In January 1914 the new state was under the International Commission of Control; public order was maintained by a gendarmerie organised with Dutch officers, while most armed men were tribal irregulars owing allegiance to local chiefs, not to the government. The value 5,000 is a PLACEHOLDER ORDER OF MAGNITUDE only, not supported by a located contemporary return. The first concrete strength figure in the Wikipedia article is 10,691 active troops in 1923 - a decade later.

secondary_research.organisation: No coherent national army in January 1914. Provisional government (Vlorë) with an Albanian National Army nominally created 4 December 1912. International Commission of Control (Great Powers) supervised the new state; Dutch officers organised the gendarmerie. Effective authority was limited to towns and the central corridor; north was governed by tribal customary law (kanun) and parts of the south by Greek-backed autonomous movements (Northern Epirus). Prince Wied (Wilhelm zu Wied) arrived only in March 1914 and the country descended into rebellion later that year.
secondary_research.garrisons: Vlorë (seat of provisional government), Tirana, Durrës (main port, international landing point), Shkodër (contested with Montenegro/Serbia), Berat and Korçë (southern centres, contested with Greece). These are administrative/nominal centres rather than verifiable military garrisons.
uncertainties: DATA RELIABILITY EXPLICITLY VERY LOW - Albania is the weakest-documented case of the five states.
The 5,000 'active' figure is an acknowledged placeholder, not a sourced fact; it should be treated as unknown within a 3,000-15,000 range.
The 0 'reserves' value means 'no organised reserve', not 'no armed population'.
The state was under international control in January 1914 and lacked effective monopoly of force.
Territorial control was disputed (Northern Epirus, Shkodër area, Korçë) and borders were not finally settled.
No reliable contemporary official statistics were accessible; US War Department 1916 handbook should be consulted if available.

active.definition: Peace-footing regular army: officers, NCOs and conscripts actually serving
active.derivation: EB1911 gives the 1908 peace strength as 1,939 officers and civilians + 19,416 NCOs and men = 21,355 (plus 2,661 horses/mules). The 1904 reorganisation scheme envisioned 1,887 officers + 25,140 men = 27,027 on a peace footing, but its full implementation was suspended in 1906 for five years. The round value 20,000 is used as the January 1914 order of magnitude; after the Balkan Wars Greece doubled its territory and retained part of its army mobilised, so the true number under arms in early 1914 may have been considerably higher.

reserves.definition: Trained reserves and National Guard available in addition to the regular peace establishment
reserves.derivation: EB1911 (1908 base) estimated reserves of about 77,000 and a territorial army of about 37,000 in war (total ~114,000); the unimplemented 1904 scheme envisioned 120,000 active + 60,000 territorial in war (180,000). During the Balkan Wars Greece fielded 125,000 in the army and had 'another 140,000 in the National Guard and reserves' (WIKI_HELLENIC_ARMY). The value 140,000 is taken as the post-Balkan-War trained reserve pool, which after territorial gains and mobilisation reforms was larger than the 1908 estimate. This remains an estimate.

secondary_research.organisation: After the 1897 defeat a reorganisation scheme was approved in June 1904 under Crown Prince Constantine: triangular infantry divisions and a large reserve/territorial army, with French military missions (1884-87 and 1911-14) training the officer corps. The 1904 law was only partially implemented (suspended 1906 for five years). Greek forces were reorganised and expanded for the Balkan Wars, adopting the triangular division, and after 1913 the army covered newly annexed Macedonia, Epirus and the Aegean islands. The exact 1914 corps/district structure is not given in the sources located; the five districts above are the principal peacetime garrison/command centres inferred from the geography and the 1913-14 army locations.
secondary_research.garrisons: Athens (capital, Evelpidon Military Academy), Piraeus (naval base and arsenal at Salamis), Larissa (Thessaly, principal northern assembly area), Thessaloniki (Salonica, captured 1912, major Macedonian garrison), Ioannina (captured 1913, Epirus garrison), Patras and Tripolis (Peloponnese), Kavala and Serres (newly acquired eastern Macedonia), Corfu and Crete (island garrisons). Greek forces remained partially mobilised in 1913-14 because of the unresolved dispute with Bulgaria.
uncertainties: The detailed peace-strength figures (1908) and reserve estimates predate the Balkan Wars and the doubling of Greek territory in 1913.
20,000 is a rounded estimate for January 1914; no dated 1914 return was located.
Post-1913 partial mobilisation against Bulgaria means actual troops under arms may have exceeded the peace establishment.
The 140,000 reserve figure refers to 1912-13 and may not be exactly applicable to January 1914.
The list of five military districts is inferred from major garrison locations, not taken from a documented 1914 order of battle.
Wartime figures (125,000-148,000) must not be used as peace strength.
